episodes.153310: A strong area of low pressure tracked to the west of the area across Western New York on the night of November 30th before stalling by the morning of December first.  A warm and moist Atlantic moisture fetch allowed for an anomalous southeasterly airmass for the beginning of December to move into the region.  Heavy rain occurred across the region with widespread reports of 2 to 3 of rain being reported across the eastern slopes of the Western Maine Mountains.  This led to localized flooding and minor damage.
episodes.153889: A strong storm system passed well to the west of southern New England on November 30th and early on December 1st.  Strong to damaging wind gusts occurred on November 30th and the entire state of Rhode Island received between 2.20 and 3.78 inches of rain. This led to street flooding, just after midnight on December 1st.
episodes.154601: A large plume of concentrated moisture or Atmospheric River (AR) with an associated low-pressure system moved across the Pacific Ocean and transported tropical moisture from the southwest which impacted Southeast Alaska (SEAK) from December 1st through December 2nd. This event brought widespread significant, and sometimes historic record setting rainfall to locations across Southeast Alaska. There were multiple waves along the main front to produce a quasi-stationary front and allowed heavy precipitation to persist over the panhandle for a long duration. Rainfall amounts were as high as over 15 at Little Port Walter with most other locations reporting 5 to 12 over the 2 days. Juneau, Skagway and Haines airports broke their all time daily precipitation record on December 1st along with the all time 2 day total when both days are combined. Rainfall intensity recurrence intervals  ranged from a 50 to 200 year event when looking at 6,12,24,48 hour time periods. In some locations the precipitation started out as snow, minor accumulations but then changed quickly over to moderate/heavy rain. Significant snowfall did occur mainly at high elevations and along the Haines and Klondike highways before transition to rain as temperatures rose above freezing all the way up to 6000 feet with the impacting warm front. Snow accumulations were very impressive from December 1st into the 2nd with 18 at 800 feet near the Haines US customs border station and a staggering 59 at 2560 feet on Mount Ripinski above Haines. There was persistent precipitation that occured the previous weeks to keep the soils on the wet side. The heavy precipitation and warm temperatures melted snow that had already accumulated on the ground at sea level then as the snow level climbed above the mountain top this increased the amount of runoff significantly from the mountains. All the excess runoff resulted in significant and in places record flooding of roads and homes, erosion that damaged roads and infrastructure, and widespread mass wasting events such as landslides and debris flows. Most of these impacts were reported to have started in the early morning hours of December 2nd and persist into December 3rd or longer. The northern half of Southeast Alaska saw most if not all of these impacts with a few specific rivers, Salmon River in Gustavus and Jordan Creek in Juneau, seeing record river stage values. Widespread damaging debris flows impacted Juneau, Skagway and Haines that took out roads, destroyed homes and caused 2 fatalities in Haines. ��To go along with the heavy precipitation there was also very strong damaging winds as the waves moved along the front over the panhandle. These strong winds damaged power lines from falling trees.��In total there were about 7 communities (Haines, Juneau, Skagway, Gustavus, Hoonah, Tenakee Springs, and Hyder) that declared a disaster from this event.
episodes.154630: Widespread heavy rain was observed across a large portion of Arkansas. This brought on an increase in river levels along the Cache. At Patterson, minor flooding was observed.
episodes.154791: Strong low pressure tracked north across Quebec province through the 1st...drawing a cold front across the region. A very strong low level jet crossed the region in advance of the front during the 1st. The strongest winds occurred along the Downeast coast. South/southeast winds along the coast were sustained at 25 to 35 mph...with gusts in excess of 60 mph. A peak wind gust of 70 mph was measured near the town of Lubec in coastal Washington county. A wind gust of 61 mph was measured at  Eastport...also in coastal Washington county. The strong winds extended up the Penobscot River Valley into southern Penobscot county where a 58 mph wind gust was reported at the Bangor Airport. The strong winds brought down trees and power lines contributing to power outages. Power outages peaked at around 17,000 customers during the morning of the 1st with the most extensive outages across portions of Hancock and Penobscot counties. Saturated ground from heavy rain contributed to the number of toppled trees. Some roads were blocked due to fallen trees and downed power lines.|Unseasonably warm air was drawn north in advance of the cold front supporting precipitation in the form of rain. Abundant moisture was also drawn north supporting heavy rain. The heaviest rain totals occurred south and east of a line from southeast Aroostook county...across northern Penobscot county to central Piscataquis county. Rain totals of 2.50 to 3.50 inches were common in that area...with local totals to around 4.00 inches. Lesser rain totals occurred northwest of that line. Rain totals of 3.00 to 4.00 inches occurred in the headwaters of the Piscataquis River Basin. This led to flooding along portions of the Piscataquis River. At Dover-Foxcroft...the river rose above flood stage during the morning of the 1st. The river crested around a foot above flood stage that afternoon. The river fell back below flood stage during the morning of the 2nd. Flooding was generally minor...though some road closures did occur. Water was reported on Route 16 near Kingsbury and on Back Road in Abbot. Otherwise...elevated stream levels and ponding of water in low lying and poor drainage areas were the major hydrologic issues.
episodes.154931: A strong area of low pressure moved directly overhead Nov 30th, bringing some strong thunderstorms across the region. This lead to a few isolated instances of flooding around the area the next day in some of the slower reacting river basins.
episodes.155008: An area of low pressure tracked to the west of the region on the evening of Nov 30th with a broad area of moderate to heavy rain and pockets of embedded convection enveloping the region.  Widespread rainfall amounts of 1 to 2 occurred with localized amounts approaching 3 in the favorable mountain upslope areas.  Partially frozen ground and dormant vegetation status led to rapid run-off into area rivers.

events.narrative: Heavy rain with measured amounts of 2.82 being reported in the vicinity of Newry, ME lead to localized flash flooding at the Sunday River Ski Resort.  In addition to the heavy rain, melting man made snow contributed to rapid runoff.  Heavy erosion and undermining caused damage to one of the base areas at Sunday River Resort.

The stream gage on the Western Branch Potomac River near Upper Marlboro reached flood stage during the specified timeframe, reaching a peak stream level of 13.13 feet at 3:15 AM EST.  At 12 feet, much of Race Track Road floods between Marlboro Pike and the community center.

Strong low pressure moved north up the spine of the Appalachians and to the west of Maine and New Hampshire resulting in 2 to 3 inches of rain on partially frozen ground.  Rapid run-off led to fast rises on the Pemigewasset. The river crested at minor flood stage early on December 1st at 10.1 ft.  The flood level is 9 ft in Woodstock.  No damage was reported.

An area of low pressure tracked to the west of the region on the night of Nov 30th with a broad area of moderate to heavy rain and pockets of embedded convection enveloping the region.  Rainfall reports of 2.5 were reported in the Swift River Basin, which led to rapid river rises.  The Swift River at Roxbury crested at 8.7 ft, minor flood stage is 7 feet. No impacts were reported.
In Warwick, there was two feet of street flooding on Jefferson Boulevard.
In East Providence, street flooding was reported on Catamore Boulevard.
Heavy rains brought flooding to the Cache River at Patterson in early Decemeber.

Strong low pressure moved north up the spine of the Appalachians and to the west of Maine and New Hampshire resulting in 2 to 3 inches of rain on partially frozen ground.  Rapid run-off led to fast rises on the Saco River. The river crested at minor flood stage early on December 1st at 10.2 ft.  The flood level is 9 ft in Conway.  No damage was reported.
Minor flooding occurred along the Pscataquis River at Dover-Foxcroft. Water was also reported over roads in several other locations.

An area of low pressure tracked to the west of the region on the night of Nov 30th with a broad area of moderate to heavy rain and pockets of embedded convection enveloping the region.  Rainfall reports of 2.5 were reported in the Kennebec River Basin, which led to rapid river rises.  The Kennebec River at Skowhegan crested in minor flood stage at 45,833 CFS, flood stage is 35,000 CFS. No significant impacts were reported.

Significant snow fell on the days leading up to December 1 and 2 with about 35 inches at sea level with much more at higher elevations. As the temperatures warm through December 2nd heavy rain fell on the snowpack to increase runoff and slope instability. There were multiple debris flows and avalanches that isolated Hyder Alaska with Stewart British Columbia Canada by blocking the only road connecting the communities for 2 days. Hyder was also without power.

The atmospheric river moved over the Glacier Bay area and Gustavus in the early morning hours of December 1st and persisted through the late evening hours of December 2nd. Heavy to moderate rainfall persisted over 36 hours with the highest amounts coming during the overnight hours going into December 2nd. In the first 12 hours of the event, 2.16 of precipitation fell which is a 5 to 10 year event, some of that precipitation did fall as snow at higher elevations. There was a few inches of snow at sea level but that quickly melted. More warm and moist air moved over the region into the evening hours of the 1st and persisted into the early morning of the 2nd. More heavy precipitation fell through this time frame and produces significant runoff as the ground was totally saturated as well as runoff from snowmelt. Precipitation totals were as high as 7.25 for the event from early December 1st through the early morning hours of December 3rd which is a 200 year event.  The 24 hour precipitation amount reported at the Gustavus CRN site on December 1st was 3.76 which is a 10 to 25 year event.  The 48 hour precipitation amount from Bartlett Cove in Glacier Bay National Park was 6.43 and Gustavus CRN reported 5.69 which is a 50-100 year event for both sites.  The magnitude of the precipitation and snowmelt overwhelmed culverts and produced record water level on the Salmon River. Roads located near the Salmon River were flooded with up to 4 feet in places as wind fall in the river directed high water into the gravel pits and into the road systems of Gustavus. The hardest hit areas were Rink Creek Rd, Wilson Rd, Toad Rd along with areas near the Salmon River. The Salmon River began to rise rapidly through the morning hours of December 1st from the first batch of heavy rainfall. The water levels continued on a steep upward trend through the morning hours of December 2nd as it crested at 17.26 feet for a total rise of over 7 feet from the extreme amount of precipitation. This was a record stage for this site which was installed by the USGS in 2014. Flooding persisted for days after the heavy rain relaxed as it took awhile for the water levels to recede from the saturated sandy soils. The city declared a disaster declaration as homes were damaged from flooding along with road infrastructure damage.

An area of low pressure tracked to the west of the region on the night of Nov 30th with a broad area of moderate to heavy rain and pockets of embedded convection enveloping the region.  Rainfall reports of 2.5 were reported in the Kennebec River Basin, which led to rapid river rises.  The Kennebec River at Augusta crested in minor flood stage at 14.1 ft, flood stage is 14 ft. No significant impacts were reported with minor low land flooding.

As the atmospheric river moved over the the central inner channels near Petersburg in the early morning hours of December 1st through the early morning of December 2nd it produced significant amount of precipitation. Through that time frame 3 to 6 of precipitation fell with the highest rain rates of .5 per hour in the morning hours of December 1st with another burst of heavy rainfall in the evening. Falls Creek along Mitkof highway in Petersburg rose quickly from the heavy precipitation along with added runoff from snowmelt at higher elevations. The creek went above minor flood stage in the late morning of December 1st and continued to climb above moderate flood stage of 24 feet in the afternoon. The creek crested at 24.38 feet for a 5 foot rise and produced some impacts to the highway. AKDOT had to close the road at times the night of December 1st due to about 8 to 10 inches of water running over the road along with debris that had to clear off the road.

As the atmospheric river moved over the Hoonah and Tenakee Springs area in the early morning hours of December 1st through mid morning of December 2nd it produced significant amount of precipitation. In the first 12 hours of the event 2.5 of precipitation fell with some of that falling as snow at higher elevations. More warm and moist air moved over the region into the evening hours of the 1st and persisted into the early morning of the 2nd. More heavy precipitation fell through this time frame and produces significant runoff as the ground was totally saturated as well as runoff from snowmelt.  The Hoonah COOP observer reported 4.70 on December 2nd a all time daily precipitation record and a 50 to 100 year event. It was also a 2 day all time precipitation record of 7.18 for December 1st and 2nd which is a 200 to 500 year event. At the Hoonah RAWS weather station, close to Tenakee Springs, it reported 6.9 in 24 hours and 8.74 in 48 hours which are both a 100-200 year event. During the heaviest precipitation of the event, the evening of December 1st, 3.7 in 12hrs was reported at the Hoonah RAWS with is a 10-25 year event. All of this heavy rainfall along with snowmelt overwhelmed the water treatment plant in Hoonah and damaged the system from debris from the runoff. Also there was extensive damage to roads and culverts from large amount of erosion and debris on roadways. From these impacts a disaster declaration was issued.
